text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Market-linked pooled superannuation trusts have recorded their most profitable financial-year performance since the 1987 stockmarket crash, posting an average investment return of 18.6 per cent after fees and tax. Mercer Investment Consulting and InTech Asset consulting released surveys yesterday detailing the performance of the superannuation industry. Page 21.

The Bass Strait Oil Trust float was launched on the Australian Stock Exchange yesterday, where a lack of interest by investors forced a discount on the issue price. After opening with a unit price of A$5 stocks declined to A$4.75 before recovering to close at A$4.90. Page 21.

Australian company Lend Lease Corporation Ltd yesterday struck a deal with US-based fund manager Capital International. Land Lease will become Capital International's exclusive agent to sell Capital's equity fund services to Australian investors. Page 22

Industry analysts predict that as gold companies attempt to shore up their operations following the recent deterioration in gold prices, they are likely to wind back investment in the exploration sector. Herald Resources director Michael Wright said yesterday that gold miners would start searching for low-cost ounces as there is currently no point looking for higher-cost ounces. Page 24.

Mt Leyshon Gold Mines Ltd yesterday recorded a 4 per cent rise in gold production, with cash costs being reduced by A$33 an ounce to A$330 an ounce. This improved performance is expected to be repeated by its parent company, Normandy Mining, which is to release details of its performance for the last financial year later this week. Page 24.

Sons of Gwalia chairman Peter Lalor said yesterday that approximately 25 Australian gold mines could be threatened with closure if the current fall in gold bullion prices continues. Lalor stressed that Sons of Gwalia, one of the industry's major companies, would begin reviewing the performance of two high cost operations at Bullfinch and Laverton. Page 25
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Australian A$350 million citrus industry is in crisis, with orange growers predicting that as much as 10 per cent of the navel crop may be dumped. Record harvests in South Australia, New South Wales and Victoria have caused prices for navel oranges used in the cordial market to plunge from a 1995 high of A$180 a tonne to A$20 a tonne.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) is nearing the completion of its investigation into film distribution practices. The ACCC was acting on complaints from independent cinema exhibitors that major film distributors were abusing their market power by forcing independent cinemas out of the industry to make way for an increasing number of multiplexes. Page 22.

Australian exporters have penetrated the profitable Japanese ferry market, with the Australian consul in Fukuoka, Peter Linford, confirming yesterday that five Australian vessels had been sold to Japanese ferry operators. The Japanese Maritime Credit Corp has approved the purchase of two ferries already, and Linford is hopeful that Australian industry will be able to sell about five ferries a year in Japan from now on. Page 23.

The ANZ Bank is expected shortly to announce the appointment of three executives to new high-level positions instituted as part of the group's global reorganisation. The positions will cover marketing, strategy, and technology and operations and will be decided later this month, although a decision on a new chief executive is not expected in the near future. Page 23.

Insurer MMI has acquired the New Zealand and Pacific Island operations of its rival FAI for A$50 million. The deal was announced yesterday and is seen as part of MMI's attempt to penetrate the international insurance market. Page 23.

Sydney-based technology group HRL has purchased national technical services provider ETRS Pty Ltd for an undisclosed amount. HRL managing director Graeme Pleasance said the acquisition would enable the company to expand its operations interstate. Page 23
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The price of gold has fallen to its lowest level in 12 years, with gold stocks losing A$1.3 billion of their value in the two trading days following the Reserve Bank's revelation that it had sold 167 tonnes of reserves in the past six months. The gold inex also dropped 93.7 points to 1275.5. Page 25.

The latest ANZ job advertisement survey revealed advertised vacancies grew only 0.5 per cent in June. The official unemployment figures for June are expected to be announced on Thursday, and ANZ's chief economist, Saul Eslake, is predicting a steady 8.8 per cent unemployment rate. Page 28.

Video distributor Network Entertainment is understood to be looking for investors to take a major share in the troubled company in an attempt to turn it around. Since Network's listing, the company has lost distribution deals with two major Hollywood studios. Page 27.

The Pilliga Scrub township of Baradine, in northern New South Wales, is busy developing a timber industry to replace the railway sleeper industry that was the town's main economic activity since the 1880s. The Gallagher Insultimber company has set up business in Baradine, specialising in export oriented ironbark value-added products. Page 29.

Brisbane-based biotechnology company Progen Industries yesterday disclosed plans to move into the US market with hopes to be listed on the US stock exchange by the end of this month. Progen's company secretary, Charles Furness, said the listing was aimed at attracting investors knowledgeable about the biotechnology sector. Page 27.

The Federal Government will be asked by the Opposition this week to reject a proposal by the Wallis report for a single prudential regulator for the financial system. The Treasury Department is believed to favour the scheme for a new Australian Prudential Regulation Commission, and lobbying over its future is set to begin in the next few weeks. Page 27.
THE AGE

A Supreme Court heard yesterday that the Budget Rent A Car Group was labouring under massive debts and was being pressed by creditors when company directors Robert Ansett and Stan Hamley signed off on a prospectus aimed at raising A$12.5 million from a public float. Ansett and Humley are now facing charges of deliberately issuing a prospectus which contained inaccurate information. Page B1.

Australian company Hoyts Cinemas is close to announcing a major cinema development in Britain, to be situated on Lend Lease's A$1 billion Bluewater project near London. Hoyts Cinemas' rival, Village Roadshow, has become an important factor in the British cinema market following its joint venture with Warner Bros, and Hoyts will be hoping to emulate its success. Page B3.

Marketing group International Media Management (Holdings) has appointed music industry identity Glenn Wheatley to its board. It is Wheatley's first involvement in a public company since he declared bankruptcy in 1993 on account of personal debts. Page B3

Wittner Shoes retail chain owner and managing director David Wittner has claimed that planned tariff cuts to the textile, clothing and footwear sectors will reduce choice for consumers. Wittner said that domestic manufacturers are essential as they react quicker to changes in consumer taste than overseas suppliers could. Page B3.

According to sharemarket analysts, gold producer Newcrest's position in a gold-for-equity deal involving ANZ Bank has deteriorated to a loss of around A$70 million. The complicated agreement which freed Newcrest from its direct 11.9 per cent stake in rival Normandy Mining also left the company open to movements in Normandy's shares over the next two years. Page B2.

Hawker chief cashes in on Jackson Bid Hawker Richardson managing director Graeme Salthouse is expected to receive around A$800,000 if he chooses to sell his scrip in the wake of the company's takeover by the Austrim group. Salthouse has a large interest in the company compared with the share held by other board members. Page B2.
